claim: Freezing is a predominant threat behavior in rats.
source: Freezing is a predominant threat behavior in rats.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: A threat cue can organize diverse behaviors beyond freezing, including locomotion.
source: We have recently shown that a threat cue can organize diverse behaviors beyond freezing, including locomotion (Chu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Conditioned suppression was only observed at higher foot shock intensities (0.35 mA and 0.50 mA).
source: We found that conditioned suppression was only observed at higher foot shock intensities (0.35 mA and 0.50 mA).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 0.50 mA and 0.35 mA shock-paired visual cues suppressed reward seeking, rearing, and scaling.
source: The 0.50 mA and 0.35 mA shock-paired visual cues suppressed reward seeking, rearing, and scaling, as well as light-directed rearing and light-directed scaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The 0.50 mA and 0.35 mA shock-paired visual cues suppressed light-directed rearing and light-directed scaling.
source: The 0.50 mA and 0.35 mA shock-paired visual cues suppressed reward seeking, rearing, and scaling, as well as light-directed rearing and light-directed scaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Shock-paired visual cues elicited locomotion and freezing.
source: These shock-paired visual cues further elicited locomotion and freezing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Ethogram data could accurately classify rats into paired and unpaired groups.
source: Linear discriminant analyses showed that ethogram data could accurately classify rats into paired and unpaired groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: Using complete ethogram data produced superior classification compared to behavior subsets, including an immobility subset featuring freezing.
source: Using complete ethogram data produced superior classification compared to behavior subsets, including an immobility subset featuring freezing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: A shock-paired cue can elicit freezing.
source: The most well-known property is that a shock-paired cue (or context) can elicit freezing (Bolles and Collier, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pavlovian conditioning procedures measuring freezing have been used to reveal neural bases of fear.
source: Pavlovian conditioning procedures measuring freezing have been used to great effect to reveal neural bases of fear (LeDoux et al., 1988; De Oca et al., 1998; Goosens and Maren, 2001; Koo et al., 2004; Monfils et al., 2009; Li et al., 2013; Massi et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A shock-paired cue can suppress reward seeking.
source: A shock-paired cue can also suppress reward seeking (Estes and Skinner, 1941), a phenomenon referred to as conditioned suppression (Killcross et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A shock-paired auditory cue elicits locomotion, rearing, and jumping, in addition to freezing.
source: Using conditioned suppression procedures, we recently demonstrated that a shock-paired auditory cue elicits locomotion, rearing, and jumping, in addition to freezing (Chu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Observing such a diversity of fear-conditioned behaviors is uncommon.
source: Though consistent with some studies (Gruene et al., 2015; Totty et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2022; Le et al., 2024; Borkar et al., 2024; Chanthongdee et al., 2024), observing such a diversity of fear-conditioned behaviors is uncommon.
evidence: Supported by citations and inference from the literature.

claim: Freezing is a predominant fear-conditioned behavior in rats across a variety of settings.
source: In rats, and across a variety of settings, freezing is a predominant fear-conditioned behavior (Lay et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Trott et al., 2022; Williams-Spooner et al., 2022; Fam et al., 2023; Ng and Sangha, 2023; Ng et al., 2024; Yau et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Neither the 0.15 mA nor the 0.25 mA foot shock intensity supported conditioned suppression to the visual cue.
source: Neither the 0.15 mA nor the 0.25 mA foot shock intensity supported conditioned suppression to the visual cue.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: Paired and unpaired rats in both 0.15 mA and 0.25 mA shock intensity conditions showed identical, decreasing suppression ratio patterns across all 20 trials.
source: Paired and unpaired rats in both shock intensity conditions showed identical, decreasing suppression ratio patterns across all 20 trials (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ANOVA for suppression ratio found no significant main effect of group (F1,24 = 3.67, p=0.067) for Experiment 1.
source: In support, ANOVA for suppression ratio [within factors: session (1–5; two pre-exposure, two conditioning, and one extinction), and trial (1–4); between factors: sex (female vs. male), group (paired vs. unpaired), and intensity (0.25 mA vs. 0.15 mA); Figure 1C] found no significant main effect of group (F1,24 = 3.67, p=0.067), and no significant group interactions: group × session (F4,96 = 0.61, p=0.66), and session × trial × group (F12,288 = 0.77, p=0.68).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Two-tailed, independent samples t-tests found no significant differences between the paired and unpaired rats receiving the 0.25 mA foot shock or the 0.15 mA foot shock for any of the 20 trials (all p>0.05).
source: Two-tailed, independent samples t-tests found no significant differences between the paired and unpaired rats receiving the 0.25 mA foot shock or the 0.15 mA foot shock for any of the 20 trials (all p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The 0.50 mA and the 0.35 mA foot shock intensities supported conditioned suppression to the visual cue.
source: By contrast, the 0.50 mA and the 0.35 mA foot shock intensities supported conditioned suppression to the visual cue.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: Paired rats increased suppression ratios over the eight conditioning trials, with elevated suppression ratios apparent during the extinction session.
source: Paired rats increased suppression ratios over the eight conditioning trials, with elevated suppression ratios apparent during the extinction session.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: Unpaired rats persisted in showing low suppression ratios during both conditioning and extinction trials.
source: Unpaired rats persisted in showing low suppression ratios during both conditioning and extinction trials.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: ANOVA for suppression ratio found a significant main effect of group (F1,24 = 37.2, p=2.66 × 10–6) for Experiment 2.
source: In support, ANOVA for suppression ratio [within factors: session (1–5; two pre-exposure, two conditioning, and one extinction), and trial (1–4); between factors: sex (female vs. male), group (paired vs. unpaired), and intensity (0.50 mA vs. 0.35 mA); Figure 1D] found a significant main effect of group (F1,24 = 37.2, p=2.66 × 10–6), a significant group × session interaction (F4,96 = 18.12, p=4.06 × 10–11), and significant group × session × trial interaction (F12,288 = 2.28, p=0.009).

claim: Six observers blind to group, sex, and intensity scored 22,272 total frames.

claim: The mean inter-rater reliability was 72.41%.
source: The mean inter-rater reliability was 72.41%.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: Inter-rater reliability was higher when fewer behaviors were present within a trial (e.g., 77.7% when three were present).

evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The inter-rater reliability remained high, at 71.9%, even when eight behaviors were present.
source: Although inter-rater reliability was higher when fewer behaviors were present within a trial (e.g., 77.7% when three were present), the inter-rater reliability remained high, at 71.9%, even when eight behaviors were present (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Disagreement rarely involved two observers assigning different, specific behaviors to a single frame.
source: Disagreement rarely involved two observers assigning different, specific behaviors to a single frame.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: Disagreement occurred when one observer assigned background to a frame while the other observer assigned a specific behavior to that frame.

evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data.

source: Group classification during cue light illumination (Figure 5E) was greater than chance for each multibehavior category, but was variable across categories: Immobile (mean ± SEM group classification, 71.39 ± 0.003%; one-sample t-test compared to 50%, p=7.35 × 10–93), Horizontal (57.80 ± 0.004%; p=1.34 × 10–32), Vertical (64.17 ± 0.004%; p=3.56 × 10–58), and Reward (61.59 ± 0.005%; p=5.75 × 10–42).

source: Critically, group classification based on the complete ethogram was superior to each category subset: (independent samples t-test, Ethogram vs. Immobile, p=5.93 × 10–25; Ethogram vs. Horizontal, p=3.66 × 10–58; Ethogram vs. Vertical, p=4.10 × 10–42; Ethogram vs. Reward, p=1.08 × 10–45).

claim: Group classification post-cue light illumination was greater than chance for each multibehavior category: Immobile (54.36 ± 0.0013%), Horizontal (71.39 ± 0.0028%), Vertical (63.58 ± 0.0036%), and Reward (54.19 ± 0.0034%).
source: Group classification post-cue light illumination (Figure 5F) was also greater than chance for each multibehavior category, but variable across categories. Relative to the cue light period, the Immobile category performed worse during the post-cue light period (mean ± SEM group classification, 54.36 ± 0.0013%; one-sample t-test compared to 50%, p=2.84 × 10–55), while the Horizontal category performed better (71.39 ± 0.0028%; p=4.27 × 10–93). The Vertical category performed similarly during the post-cue light period (63.58 ± 0.0036%; p=2.99 × 10–60), while the Reward category performed worse (54.19 ± 0.0034%; p=4.63 × 10–22).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the Results section and supported by linear discriminant analysis results shown in Figure 5F.
